opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that you need both, and the question is really about what each one is good for.

Simulation has enormous advantages. You can run thousands of copies in parallel, you can run faster than real time, and the robot can fall over a million times without breaking anything or hurting anyone. For something like legged locomotion, that's been transformative. In our own work on quadruped walking, we trained policies entirely in simulation and then transferred them to a real robot. The key idea was that you don't try to make the simulator perfect. Instead, you vary the physics a lot during training, things like friction, payload, terrain, motor strength, and you train the policy to adapt online. It learns to infer, from its own recent history of states and actions, what kind of world it's in, and adjust within a fraction of a second. So the robot isn't relying on the simulator being right. It's relying on having seen enough variety that the real world looks like just another sample.

But simulation has real limits. Locomotion works well because the physics that matters, mostly rigid body dynamics and contact with the ground, can be captured reasonably well. Once you get to manipulation, deformable objects, cloth, liquids, granular materials, or the incredible richness of what the world actually looks like, simulators fall short. You also can't simulate the long tail of things that happen in a real home or a real outdoor environment. Nobody is going to model every kind of grass or every kind of kitchen.

So my view is: use simulation to get the basic motor competence, the stuff that's like what a baby or a young animal learns early through lots of trial and error. Then the real world has to take over. The robot should keep learning from its actual experience, adapting and fine-tuning as it goes. And I'd add that there's a third source people sometimes underweight, which is learning from watching. Humans have produced huge amounts of video of people doing things. A robot can learn a lot about how the world works and how hands interact with objects from that, even if the embodiment differs.

If I think about it from a developmental perspective, children don't learn in a simulator, of course, but they do a lot of cheap, safe exploration, and they learn a lot by observing others. Simulation is our engineering substitute for that cheap exploration. It's a tool, not the destination. The destination is a robot that keeps learning in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response says robots need both simulation and real-world training, using simulation to build basic competence and real-world experience to continue learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that you need both, but for different reasons, and the balance depends a lot on what part of the robot you're trying to train.

Let me start with why simulation is so attractive. The fundamental problem in robot learning is data. In computer vision, we had ImageNet, we had billions of images on the internet, and that abundance of data is what made the deep learning revolution possible. Robots don't have that. Every real-world trial takes time, the hardware wears out, things break, and you need a human standing nearby to reset the scene. So if you can get even a fraction of the benefit from simulation, where you can run thousands of parallel environments and generate years of experience in a day, that's enormously valuable.

And we've seen that it actually works for certain problems. Legged locomotion is the clearest example. Our work on quadrupeds walking over rough terrain, and more recently on humanoid walking, was trained almost entirely in simulation and then transferred to real hardware. The reason it works is that the physics of a robot's own body, its joints, its mass distribution, is something we understand reasonably well. Rigid body dynamics is a mature field. So the gap between simulated and real is small enough that with some randomization of parameters, the policy generalizes.

Where simulation gets much harder is when the robot has to interact with the rest of the world, especially through manipulation. Contact is notoriously difficult to simulate accurately. Deformable objects, cloth, liquids, friction that varies across a surface, all of these are places where simulators are either wrong or very expensive. And perception is another gap. Rendering has gotten much better, but there's still a difference between a rendered kitchen and a real kitchen with its clutter and lighting and the particular way light reflects off a wet counter.

So my view is that simulation is where you learn the things about the robot itself, the control, the proprioception, the basic motor skills. And the real world is where you learn about the world, the objects, the variability, the long tail of situations you could never have anticipated in a simulator. I like to think about this in terms of how children develop. There's a lot of sensorimotor learning in the first year that's about discovering your own body, and then there's a long period of learning about the environment through interaction. Those are different kinds of learning.

The practical recipe that I think is emerging is pretrain in simulation, then fine-tune with real data. The simulation gives you a strong prior so you aren't starting from scratch, and the real-world data corrects for the mismatch. The question of how much real data you need is really the crux, and the field is working hard to bring that number down, whether through better sim-to-real techniques, through teleoperation data, or through learning from video of humans.

I'd also add one caution. There's a tendency to treat the simulator as ground truth and optimize relentlessly against it, and then be surprised when the policy exploits some artifact of the physics engine. The simulator is a model, and all models are wrong in some way. So you should always keep the real world in the loop as the final arbiter. Nature doesn't care how well your policy did in your simulator.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly says robot training needs both simulation and real-world training, and explains their distinct roles.

astra-6.text:
I think we need both. Simulation is very useful because you can try many things cheaply, and you can make mistakes without breaking the robot. But the question is always: how well does what you learn in simulation transfer to the real world?

For some problems, the simulator can be quite good. For manipulation, where contact and friction matter, it is much harder. A robot might learn to exploit some peculiarity of the simulator that simply doesn’t exist in reality.

So I would use simulation to get started, to explore and learn useful behaviors, but then bring the robot into the real world to refine those behaviors and test them. The ultimate measure is whether the robot can actually do the task. Success in simulation is useful evidence, but it isn’t the end goal.

r001.rationale: The candidate says “we need both” and describes using simulation to get started, then refining and testing behaviors in the real world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need both. Simulation is useful because you can generate a lot of experience cheaply. A robot can try something thousands of times without breaking equipment, and you can control the conditions to understand what it is learning.

But the difficulty is that the simulator is itself a model of the world. In manipulation, for example, contact, friction, and the properties of an object can make a big difference. A policy can become very good at exploiting the simulator and still fail on a real robot.

So I would use simulation to learn useful initial behaviors, then use real-world experience to adapt and test them. The balance will depend on the task and how faithfully we can simulate the relevant physics. Ultimately, if we want robots to work in the real world, that is where we have to measure success.

r001.rationale: The response says “we need both” and describes using simulation for initial behaviors followed by real-world experience to adapt and test them.
